The applicant alleged that the monitoring of his medical correspondence while he was in prison breached his right to respect for his correspondence and private life under Article 8 of the convention. The case was decided to examine the merits of the application at the same time as its admissibility. The applicant wished to correspond confidentially with his external medical specialist to ensure that he would receive the necessary medical treatment and supervision in prison. He expressed his concerns about his medical correspondence being read and applied to the prison governor for a direction that such correspondence should be accorded confidentiality. The prison governor agreed that the applicant’s medical correspondence would not be read provided that certain conditions were met. All outgoing and incoming mail was to be marked “medical in confidence”. The applicant wanted reassurance from the medical specialist who was involved in treating him and from whom he required continual medical care. Mr Justice [PERSON] found that the initial decision of the prison governor to enable the applicant to correspond on a confidential basis with his external medical specialist indicated that it was reasonable to permit such confidential correspondence. The Court of Appeal concluded that although the procedure set out in the prison governors’ letter of [DATE_TIME] amounted to an interference with the applicant’s right to respect for his correspondence, the interference was justified and proportionate. The Court of Appeal concluded that the monitoring of the applicant’s medical correspondence was a proportionate interference with his Article 8 rights. It did not exclude the possibility that in another case it might be disproportionate to refuse confidentiality to medical correspondence in the prison context. It was recognised that there was an inescapable risk of abuse, for example, if for example the prison medical officer should know about it. The interference in question had not denied the essence of the applicants’ rights as it related to one correspondent only. The applicant’s petition for leave to appeal was refused by the House of Lords on the ground that the petition did not raise an arguable point of law of general public importance. Since [DATE_TIME] the applicant has been located in a Category B prison in [LOCATION]. The applicant is currently serving a sentence of life in prison with a minimum term of 15 years.

rewrited_text: The case originated in an application (no. 23883/06) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) The applicants alleged that their eviction from their flat following their refusal to remove a satellite dish resulted in violations of Articles 8 and 10 of the convention. The Swedish Government (‘the Government’) was represented by their Agent. Landlord sought execution of the notice of termination, claiming that the applicants' satellite installation violated the express ban in Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. The applicants, as well as the other tenants summoned, contested the landlord's claims before the Rent Review Board. They stated that, by mounting satellite dishes for the reception of television programmes, some of which were broadcast in their mother tongues, they were exercising their freedom to receive information. The Rent Review Board gave a decision on [DATE_TIME] finding in their favour. The landlord appealed to the Svea Court of Appeal. The court held an oral hearing at which, inter alia, Mr [PERSON] gave evidence. It also made an inspection of the applicants' satellite installation. By a final decision, the court found that the applicants had disregarded their obligations as tenants. The court found that the applicants' dish was virtually always positioned outside the kitchen window and thus constituted a permanent installation. It concluded, contrary to the findings of the Rent Review Board, that its placement breached Rule 13 of the tenancy agreement. Although their satellite installation did not pose any real safety threat, their interests could not be allowed to override the weighty and reasonable interest of the landlord that order and good custom be upheld.

Byggettan was obliged to pay fees for monitoring the wages of its members. Two of the workers claimed the fees exceeded the costs of the work. The case was taken to the Labour Court, which ruled that the fees were not required to be paid to the workers. The Court found that the deductions violated the right to freedom of association under Article 11 of the Convention and Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights. The judge also found that it was not mandatory for the workers to pay for the fees. However, he said that they would have to pay them if they had chosen to do so. The workers appealed the decision, and the case was eventually settled out of court. The court found in favour of the applicants.
